Wikipedia claims some people (though not who, seems to show up in pop sci writing) do in fact refer to the inner/outer core boundary that way, but that's not what most seismologists would think of if you said it.

We probably should consider the Gutenberg discontinuity as the seismic representation of the thermal-rheological Lithosphere-Asthenosphere Boundary like we consider the Mohorovičić discontinuity as the seismic expression of the compositional Crust-Mantle Boundary, but we're usually not that careful.

The Gutenberg discontinuity named for German seismologist Beno Gutenberg (he moved to America in 1930 after having his career blocked due to his Jewish heritage, see link).

This discontinuity is more commonly known as the Lithosphere-Asthenosphere Boundary or LAB, and is a global feature.

The Lehmann discontinuity named for Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann (more famous for her work showing the existence of the inner core, see link).

Appears to be global but highly variable in depth, which makes it very difficult to understand. Related to the asthenosphere in some way.

The Conrad discontinuity named for Austrian geophysicist Victor Conrad (was one of the intellectuals of Jewish descent who fled central Europe immediately prior to WW2, see link).

Often seen in continental crust, but not oceanic, maybe related to the shift from felsic to mafic rocks, or not.

The Mohorovičić discontinuity named for Croatian (well, technically Yugoslavian) geophysicist Andrija Mohorovičić (see link).

Often shortened to "Moho," we know it represents a change from seismic velocities typical of felsic/mafic rocks to those typical of ultramafic rocks--the crust and mantle.

Seismic discontinuities named for people, listed in approximately our order of understanding them:
-the Mohorovičić discontinuity
-the Conrad discontinuity
-the Lehmann discontinuity
-technically the Gutenberg discontinuity
